newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Gore, in S. Korea, says North Korea collapsing.
newsitem.headline: Gore, in S. Korea, says North Korea collapsing.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore, injecting urgency into a mission to bring Pyongyang into peace talks, declared during a visit to South Korea on Saturday the communist North was near collapse.
Meanwhile, North Korea turned up the heat on its demands for food in return for peace talks.

Communist leaders, apparently using a well-tried tactic by raising the spectre of a military menace, told visiting U.S. senators unless aid was forthcoming the powerful military could block the latest moves towards detente.
On the second day of his visit to South Korea, Gore toured the heavily fortified Demilitarized Zone that splits the Korean peninsula under an armistice agreement that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
Gazing into North Korea, where international aid agencies report famine is just weeks away, he was asked about tensions with one of the world's last communist outposts.
"It's still real here," he said. "The Cold War survives but perhaps not for long because their system is collapsing."

Gore inspected border sites protected by units of the 37,000-strong U.S. military force in South Korea after meeting President Kim Young-sam to hone a joint strategy on dealing with the impoverished North.

Kim and U.S. President Bill Clinton jointly proposed four-way peace talks, also including China, last April in an effort to engineer a peace mechanism to replace a truce that has frozen the two Koreas in hostile confrontation.
Seoul officials reported North Korea offered its first response to the proposal on Wednesday by demanding substantial food aid at a meeting in New York.
The United States and South Korea insisted there could be no preconditions to the talks but suggested more aid could flow once talks began.
At a news conference in Tokyo, five members of a U.S. Senate team that spent 24 hours in Pyongyang reported a rift between civilian rulers and the military over the talks.
"I think that we were led to believe that there is a rift," said delegation leader Ted Stevens (R-Alaska), chairman of the Senate Appropriations Committee, a key player in U.S. aid efforts.
"The military is disturbed that the civilian authorities have not been able to obtain the food and fuel they'd been told they'd get."
The sticking point was 1.5 million tonnes of food which North Korea says was promised in a 1994 pact with the United States under which it froze its nuclear arms programme.
"Our hosts in North Korea stressed their concerns that insufficient progress had been made in fulfilling the terms of the 1994 agreed framework," the senators said in a statement.
The senators met North Korean First Vice Foreign Minister Kang Sok-ju and Kim Kye Gwan, a member of the Foreign Affairs Committee. Both men are regarded as close to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il.
Military officials snubbed the group of five.
"We regret that we did not meet with officials of the Korean People's Army," the statement said.
"Failure by the North Korean military to support and participate in the negotiations .... could pose an insurmountable obstacle."
Stevens said it was not clear whether the talk of a rift "was just rattling the cage for us or whether it was stated as a fear".
"But it was a flat statement that they were worried about the reaction of their military if we were unable to assure them that they would receive the assistance they sought."
The other senators, all members of the appropriations committee, were Daniel Inouye (D-Hawaii), Thad Cochran (R-Mississippi), Pete Domenici (R-New Mexico) and Pat Roberts (R-Kansas).
Gore arrived in South Korea on Friday from China, where he raised the issue of peace talks with President Jiang Zemin. He left Seoul after his border tour on Saturday.
